doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

chapter: Denver youth and University of Denver
title: Standards for today's students and dance-job crossover tunes
summary: Ricker discusses standards as repertoire for Eastman students and slipping tunes like Giant Steps as a rumba into dance gigs.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I’m going to leapfrog a few decades. Is learning tunes for the current jazz student as important as it was back then? The reason I’m asking is partly technology that a student now can have hundreds of tunes on their phones or on their iPad, and it’s been my experience that they seem less inclined to memorize things.

I don’t know. The standard tunes, it’s sort of like if you’re playing classical clarinet let’s say, you still study Mozart, you know and Weber, and older composers. And the standard tunes are sort of a repertoire that I know our students at Eastman develop and work on. But you know they don’t stay stuck in playing standard tunes. They are also moving into their own thing, and using the information and the skills that they develop you know as playing by ear and learning these different standards. They apply that to their compositions. So there’s sort of a couple of different tracks there. There’s the tunes you would play a dance job, that’s what we called them okay? And then there’s the jazz tunes, which were different. But you could fake it a little bit. There was some crossover ones like “The Girl from Ipanema” was one of those tunes that would cross. Or we would even, you know, play “Giant Steps” as a rumba. This is after things had been livened up a little bit at the party, and you know, you could slide something like that in in the middle of “Besame Mucho” or something.
And you could always play a nice shuffle blues and get people on the dance floor that way and just sort of get to blow on that.
